howToRead: Navy racks run in rows of three, from the wearer’s right, which is the left side of this rack. The top row is short when the number of ribbons is not divisible by three.

A star or an oak leaf is not extra decoration. It counts awards. A silver star on the Good Conduct Medal replaces five gold stars. Two bronze stars on a campaign medal are campaign phases, not two more medals. The Navy E uses a letter instead of a star.
timelineLead: Assignments sit on the first track, including the tours that overlap a longer command. Deployments are the second track. Schools and the dated career events are marks, not bars, because only a start month or a single day was recorded.
uniformsLead: Grouped by type, in the order worn within each group.
mapLead: Pins are numbered in the order of the record, and the list below uses the same numbers. Red pins are commands and assignments, blue pins are deployment bases, and yellow pins are port visits, exercises, schools, transit stopovers and other stops. Use the buttons above the map to show one group or any mix. Play walks that same list, one stop at a time, so the finished 2018 map is not the first frame. A dashed ring means the location is approximate; where a year was not recorded, the period comes from the command at the time and says so. Pins that sit close together are nudged apart slightly so each number can be read.
sourcesLead: Years, units, and campaign phases come from the shadowbox worksheet. Award counts, schools, and specialties come from the service record.
equipmentLead: Body armor, helmets, weapons, comms and crypto gear, vehicles, and ships and boats, grouped by type. Most photographs are public-domain U.S. military or National Cryptologic Museum images of the same kind of item, not his own; the Hilux and Land Cruiser photos are Creative Commons. Credits are on the Sources page.
